buyer_question: Several of our CLI tools pin docopt==0.6.2 — does the pinned package still install and behave as the README documents on a current Python, is the README's CI badge and 'tested with' statement meaningful today, and can the bundled test suite still be run with the documented commands?

claims.text: The package can be installed from PyPI with the exact command `pip install docopt==0.6.2`, after which `from docopt import docopt` succeeds and `docopt.__version__` is '0.6.2'.
claims.source_quote:
Use `pip <http://pip-installer.org>`_ or easy_install::

    pip install docopt==0.6.2
claims.probe_hint: python3 -m venv /tmp/v && /tmp/v/bin/pip install docopt==0.6.2 && /tmp/v/bin/python -c 'import docopt; from docopt import docopt as d; print(docopt.__version__)'

claims.text: docopt.py is self-contained: the single file at the pinned commit imports only Python standard-library modules and works when dropped into a project without installing anything.
claims.source_quote:
Alternatively, you can just drop ``docopt.py`` file into your
project--it is self-contained.
claims.probe_hint: curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/docopt/docopt/8fea867d4220f1095dae9d6264ec5aa4031fb712/docopt.py -o /tmp/d/docopt.py && grep -n -E '^(import|from) ' /tmp/d/docopt.py && cd /tmp/d && python3 -c 'from docopt import docopt; print(docopt("Usage: x [-v]", argv=["-v"]))'

claims.text: The docopt project tests docopt on Python 2.7, 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6 (its CI configuration targets those interpreters and CI actually runs).
The Travis CI badge at the top of the README (travis-ci.org/docopt/docopt, branch master) asserts that master currently builds and passes on Travis CI.
claims.probe_hint: curl -sL 'https://travis-ci.org/docopt/docopt.svg?branch=master' | grep -o -E '>[^<>]+<'  # record what the badge actually renders (expect 'build unknown')

claims.text: In a clone of the repository, `python setup.py test` runs docopt's unit tests.
claims.source_quote:
Testing
======================================================================

You can run unit tests using the command:

    python setup.py test
claims.probe_hint: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/docopt/docopt /tmp/docopt && cd /tmp/docopt && python3 -m venv .v && .v/bin/pip install setuptools pytest && .v/bin/python setup.py test  # setuptools >= 72 disabled the test command

claims.text: In a clone of the repository, the bundled test suite (test_docopt.py plus the language-agnostic testcases.docopt collected by conftest.py) runs and passes under a current pytest.
claims.source_quote:
A Language-agnostic test suite is bundled
with `Python implementation <http://github.com/docopt/docopt>`_.
claims.probe_hint: cd /tmp/docopt && .v/bin/pip install pytest && .v/bin/pytest -q  # conftest.py uses pytest_collect_file(path, parent) and direct Node construction; see docopt/docopt#483

the return dictionary will be:

.. code:: python

claims.text: The public API is a single function with signature `docopt(doc, argv=None, help=True, version=None, options_first=False)`.
claims.source_quote:
.. code:: python

    docopt(doc, argv=None, help=True, version=None, options_first=False)

``docopt`` takes 1 required and 4 optional arguments:

claims.text: When `docopt()` is given a version argument and the usage pattern mentions --version, invoking the program with `--version` prints the supplied version string and exits.
claims.source_quote:
- ``version``, by default ``None``, is an optional argument that
  specifies the version of your program. If supplied, then, (assuming
  ``--version`` option is mentioned in usage pattern) when parser
  encounters the ``--version`` option, it will print the supplied
  version and terminate.
claims.probe_hint: python3 -c "from docopt import docopt; docopt('Usage: p [--version]', argv=['--version'], version='2.1.0rc1')"; echo exit=$?  # expect '2.1.0rc1' on stdout and exit 0

claims.text: For a usage pattern `Usage: my_program.py [-v | -vv | -vvv]`, parsing the argv ['-vv'] yields args['-v'] == 2 (repeated flags are counted).
claims.source_quote:
If your pattern allows to match argument-less option (a flag) several
times::

    Usage: my_program.py [-v | -vv | -vvv]

then number of occurrences of the option will be counted. I.e.
``args['-v']`` will be ``2`` if program was invoked as ``my_program
-vv``.
claims.probe_hint: python3 -c "from docopt import docopt; a=docopt('Usage: my_program.py [-v | -vv | -vvv]', argv=['-vv']); assert a['-v']==2, a"

claims.text: For a usage pattern `Usage: my_program.py <file> <file> --path=<path>...`, parsing `file1 file2 --path=./here --path=./there` yields args['<file>'] == ['file1', 'file2'] and args['--path'] == ['./here', './there'].
claims.source_quote:
Usage: my_program.py <file> <file> --path=<path>...

I.e. invoked with ``my_program.py file1 file2 --path=./here
--path=./there`` the returned dict will contain ``args['<file>'] ==
['file1', 'file2']`` and ``args['--path'] == ['./here', './there']``.
claims.probe_hint: python3 -c "from docopt import docopt; a=docopt('Usage: my_program.py <file> <file> --path=<path>...', argv=['file1','file2','--path=./here','--path=./there']); assert a['<file>']==['file1','file2'] and a['--path']==['./here','./there'], a"

claims.text: A `[default: ./here ./there]` value on a repeatable option is split on whitespace into ['./here', './there'], while the same default on a non-repeatable option stays the string './here ./there'.
claims.source_quote:
# will be ['./here', './there']
    --repeatable=<arg>          [default: ./here ./there]

    # will be ['./here']
    --another-repeatable=<arg>  [default: ./here]

    # will be './here ./there', because it is not repeatable
    --not-repeatable=<arg>      [default: ./here ./there]
claims.probe_hint:
python3 -c "from docopt import docopt; d='''Usage: p [--repeatable=<arg> --repeatable=<arg>] [--not-repeatable=<arg>]

--repeatable=<arg>      [default: ./here ./there]
--not-repeatable=<arg>  [default: ./here ./there]
'''; a=docopt(d, argv=[]); assert a['--repeatable']==['./here','./there'] and a['--not-repeatable']=='./here ./there', a"
